optionRationales.a: A funnel guides liquid into a narrow opening.
optionRationales.b: A ruler measures length.
optionRationales.c: A paintbrush is not designed to guide water into a bottle.

activities.prompt: What does the capacity of a cup tell you?

optionRationales.a: Capacity tells how much a container can hold.
optionRationales.b: Colour describes appearance.
optionRationales.c: Loudness describes sound.

activities.prompt: What happens when salt is stirred into water?

options.text: It dissolves and spreads through the water
It floats forever as a lump

optionRationales.a: Salt dissolves in water and spreads through it.
optionRationales.b: Salt does not turn into a stone.
optionRationales.c: Most salt grains are no longer visible after dissolving.

activities.prompt: Which material does not dissolve easily in water?

optionRationales.a: Sand does not dissolve in water.
optionRationales.b: Sugar dissolves in water.
optionRationales.c: Salt dissolves in water.

activities.prompt: When sugar dissolves, is the sugar still in the water?

options.text: Yes, it is spread through the water

optionRationales.a: Dissolved sugar remains in the solution.
optionRationales.b: Dissolving does not destroy sugar.
optionRationales.c: Sugar does not turn water into oil.

activities.prompt: What usually happens when cooking oil and water are poured together?

optionRationales.a: Oil and water usually form separate layers.
optionRationales.b: Oil does not dissolve in water.
optionRationales.c: The mixture remains liquid.

activities.prompt: Which action can help sugar dissolve faster in water?

optionRationales.a: Stirring helps sugar spread through the water faster.
optionRationales.b: A stone does not help sugar dissolve.
optionRationales.c: Sand does not help sugar dissolve.

activities.prompt: Which is a natural source of heat and light?

optionRationales.a: The Sun provides natural heat and light.
optionRationales.b: A chair is not a heat source.
optionRationales.c: A glass cup is not a heat source.

activities.prompt: A cooking pot is on a hot stove. What should a child do?

options.text: Touch the pot to test it
Stay away and tell an adult

optionRationales.a: Staying away and telling an adult is safe.
optionRationales.b: Touching a hot pot can cause a burn.
optionRationales.c: A child should not move a hot pot.

activities.prompt: What can happen to an ice cube in a warm place?

optionRationales.a: Heat can make ice melt into liquid water.
optionRationales.b: Ice does not become stone.
optionRationales.c: Ice does not grow into a plant.

activities.prompt: You see smoke coming from a room. What is safest?

options.text: Move away and alert a trusted adult

optionRationales.a: Move away and alert an adult immediately.
optionRationales.b: A child must not enter a smoky room.
optionRationales.c: Staying near smoke is dangerous.

activities.prompt: A cup of hot water spills. What should a child do?

options.text: Move away and tell an adult

optionRationales.a: Moving away and getting adult help prevents burns.
optionRationales.b: Hot water can burn skin.
optionRationales.c: Hot water is not safe to play with.

activities.prompt: Which object is Earth's natural satellite?

optionRationales.a: The Moon travels around Earth.
optionRationales.b: Clouds are made of tiny water droplets or ice crystals.
optionRationales.c: A mountain is part of Earth's surface.

activities.prompt: Which object makes its own light?

optionRationales.a: Stars produce their own light.
optionRationales.b: The Moon reflects sunlight.
optionRationales.c: A mirror reflects light from another source.

activities.prompt: Why can we see the Moon shining in the night sky?

options.text: It reflects light from the Sun

optionRationales.a: Sunlight reflects from the Moon toward Earth.
optionRationales.b: The Moon is not a lamp.
optionRationales.c: The Moon is not made of fire.

activities.prompt: Can the Moon sometimes be seen during the daytime?

optionRationales.a: The Moon can be visible in daytime when it is above the horizon and bright enough.
optionRationales.b: The Moon is not visible only at night.
optionRationales.c: Storms do not determine whether the Moon can be seen.

activities.prompt: What is a crater on the Moon?

options.text: A round hollow or dent on its surface

optionRationales.a: A crater is a hollow or bowl-shaped mark on the Moon's surface.
optionRationales.b: The Moon has no flowing rivers like Earth.
optionRationales.c: Trees do not grow on the Moon.

activities.prompt: How did many Moon craters form?

options.text: Space rocks hit the Moon's surface

optionRationales.a: Impacts by space rocks made many craters.
optionRationales.b: Rain does not form the Moon's craters.
optionRationales.c: Wind does not make impact craters.

activities.prompt: Which model could show how a crater forms?

options.text: A child touches a hot pan
An adult drops a small ball into soft modelling dough

optionRationales.a: A supervised model can show how an impact leaves a mark.
optionRationales.b: Hot pans are dangerous and unrelated.
optionRationales.c: Unknown liquids should not be handled.

activities.prompt: What shape is a simple impact crater often like?

optionRationales.a: Many impact craters are roughly circular and bowl-shaped.
optionRationales.b: A crater is not a river.
optionRationales.c: A crater is not a tower.

activities.prompt: What is a constellation?

options.text: A pattern of stars seen in the sky
A line drawn on the Moon

optionRationales.a: A constellation is a pattern formed by stars as seen from Earth.
optionRationales.b: Clouds are not constellations.
optionRationales.c: A constellation is not a line on the Moon.

activities.prompt: Do stars in a constellation have to be close together in space?

options.text: No, they can be very far apart
They are all on the Moon

optionRationales.a: Stars that look close in a pattern can be at very different distances.
optionRationales.b: The stars do not physically touch because of the pattern.
optionRationales.c: Constellation stars are not on the Moon.

activities.prompt: How can you compare the night sky on two evenings?

options.text: Record what you see on both evenings
Change the names of the stars

optionRationales.a: Recording observations on both evenings allows comparison.
optionRationales.b: A guess is not an observation.
optionRationales.c: Changing names does not compare the sky.

activities.prompt: What should you do if clouds hide the stars?

options.text: Climb a tree to get closer
Look at the Sun through a telescope
Record that the sky was cloudy

optionRationales.a: Recording the actual observation is honest science.
optionRationales.b: Climbing a tree is unsafe.
optionRationales.c: Never look directly at the Sun, including through a telescope.
